questions.text: How should an architect address stormwater management under the checked environmental sources?

options.text: Assume DAO 2003-30 gives one universal gutter detail
Treat it as a design and mitigation issue to be coordinated through EIA, EMP, and project documents when impacts require it
Ignore it unless the contractor asks
Treat it as unrelated to environmental review

questions.rationale: The source supports impact assessment and mitigation planning, not a one-size stormwater detail.
questions.code_citation: DAO 2003-30 (or specify exact NBC section if citing building code stormwater provisions)

questions.text: What happens if a project is located in an environmentally sensitive area?

options.text: It automatically avoids DENR review
Screen whether it is in an ECA and whether Category B ECC processing applies
It automatically becomes Category D
It needs only a private owner waiver

questions.rationale: DAO 2003-30 uses ECA sensitivity as a key category factor.
questions.explanation: Dangerously incorrect; protected areas and sensitive ecosystems have strict development restrictions. False; projects in sensitive areas cannot proceed without significant restrictions and environmental review. Incomplete; biodiversity and habitat protection are primary concerns beyond flooding in sensitive areas. DENR heavily restricts or prohibits development in sensitive ecological areas; if allowed, projects face minimal footprint limits, specialized construction methods, and environmental offset requirements (reforestation, habitat restoration). Biodiversity-sensitive sites face severe development restrictions or outright prohibition—confirm site eligibility before committing to design and budget.

questions.text: What should an architect do early in pre-design regarding environmental requirements?

options.text: Wait until occupancy inspection
Screen ECP/ECA status and identify ECC, CNC, EIA, and EMP implications before fixing the site plan
Let the contractor guess the environmental category
Avoid documenting environmental assumptions

questions.rationale: The procedural manual places initial self-screening at concept or pre-feasibility.
questions.explanation: Reckless approach; discovering EIA requirements after design is advanced wastes time and money. Too late; environmental constraints must inform the design, not be addressed after construction starts. Incorrect scope; urban and suburban projects also trigger EIA and environmental restrictions depending on site conditions and project type. Architects must verify early whether a site is in a protected area or requires EIA; failure to do so can waste design time and cause costly project delays. Before design begins, confirm EIA applicability and site environmental sensitivity to avoid redesigns or project denial later.

questions.text: How should habitat-offset questions be handled in this Batch 103 article?

options.text: Invent an automatic offset percentage
Do not claim an offset rule unless a checked local primary source supports it
Say offsets are never possible
Use a marketing sustainability plan as the legal source

questions.rationale: The checked DAO anchors support impact and mitigation review but not a specific habitat-offset rule.
questions.explanation: Incorrectly assumes no responsibility; projects impacting habitat must provide environmental offsets. Incomplete; while financial contributions may be part of offsets, physical restoration (reforestation, habitat dedication) is typically required. Incorrect scope; both government and private projects must provide environmental offsets if habitat is impacted. Environmental offsets for habitat impacts include reforestation, habitat restoration on the site or elsewhere, and dedication of conservation land—these are physical mitigation measures, not just financial. Environmental offsets can require setting aside project land for conservation or restoring habitat elsewhere—impacts site planning and buildable area.

questions.text: What is an Environmental Impact Assessment in source-safe terms?

options.text: A final occupancy certificate
A process for predicting environmental consequences and designing mitigation or enhancement measures
A contractor billing format
A purely architectural style review

questions.rationale: The DAO source defines EIA around likely impacts and mitigation or enhancement measures.
questions.explanation: Confuses EIA with promotional material; EIA is a technical environmental analysis required by law for certain projects. Confuses EIA with a budget item; EIA is an environmental impact study, not a cost document. Confuses EIA with design documentation; EIA is a separate regulatory analysis that informs design, not the design itself. EIA is the systematic process of identifying, predicting, and evaluating environmental effects of a proposed project before construction proceeds (DAO 2003-30). EIA is a mandatory environmental review process, not a marketing document or cost estimate.

questions.text: How should an architect discuss EIA approval duration?

options.text: Guarantee approval in a fixed number of days for every project
Avoid promising fixed duration and recognize that stated timelines are EMB review processes
Ignore EMB processing entirely
Treat client pressure as approval

questions.rationale: The DAO operating principles state that timelines refer to EMB processes and exclude proponent preparation work.

questions.text: What local-source term should replace unsupported protected-area-system claims in this article?

options.text: A social-media map
Environmentally Critical Area screening under the EIS System
A private subdivision rule only
A contractor convenience zone

questions.rationale: The checked sources support ECA screening; other protected-area-system details need separate sources.
questions.explanation: Confuses site environmental status with architectural licensing; the Board of Architecture does not maintain environmental designations. Wrong agency; no such authority; environmental designations are maintained by DENR, not a construction industry authority. Wrong function; the Department of Budget and Management handles government finances, not environmental designations. NIPAS (National Integrated Protected Areas System) and DENR Regional Offices maintain maps and information on protected areas, biodiversity hotspots, and sensitive ecosystems. Consult NIPAS and DENR Regional Offices to determine if a proposed site is in a protected or sensitive area before proceeding with design.

questions.text: What construction documents should reflect environmental commitments when required?

options.text: Only a rendering note
Accepted EMP and mitigation commitments translated into plans, specifications, and construction-phase controls
Only a sales brochure
Only verbal instructions to the contractor

questions.rationale: Environmental commitments must be carried into project documentation when they affect design and construction.

questions.text: What is the difference between Category A and Category B under DAO 2003-30?

options.text: Category A is always exempt and Category B is always residential
Category A covers environmentally critical projects; Category B covers non-ECP projects located in environmentally critical areas
Category A needs only CNC and Category B needs no review
There is no difference

questions.rationale: The DAO category definitions distinguish ECPs from projects in ECAs.

options.text: The architect's portfolio
DENR DAO 2003-30 and its Revised Procedural Manual for the EIS System
A private subdivision manual only
